For a long time there have been rumors that Apple is developing a foldable clamshell device, which could be an iPad, a Mac, one of each, or some hybrid of the two.

Recently there were reports that, although this had been a priority project for incoming CEO John Ternus, the project has been shelved—but I don't think that's quite accurate…

Personally, I think the concept of a hybrid Mac and iPad is essentially a thing of the past. Today's Mac can run iPhone and iPad apps, and for many of us iPhone Mirroring is another tool that achieves the same end. We're also seeing increasing convergence between the operating systems, and I believe that trend will continue: we're well past the point where Apple used to argue we were merging a fridge and a toaster.

But I do think that once we have a technology that makes a software keyboard a viable replacement for a hardware keyboard, we'll ultimately end up with an all-screen foldable Mac. It won't happen soon, but it will happen.

Medium-term: the dynamic keyboard

I think it's still a long way off because I believe there will be an interim stage, and that's the dynamic hardware keyboard. I talked about why I think that's the future as long ago as a decade, and although the technology exists in some niche applications, it hasn't yet gone mainstream.

One early attempt was the Sonder Keyboard, which used tiny e-ink displays to remap the labels and functions of the keys.

For someone who spends all day editing in Final Cut Pro, a QWERTY keyboard is of very little use, which is why there's a market for physical keyboards and keyboard covers.

How smart would it be if our MacBook keyboard, or our desktop Magic Keyboard, could automatically re-label itself according to the app in use at the time?

A software keyboard that feels like a hardware one

However, the longer-term goal is a fully software keyboard. Back in 2016 I argued that the case Steve Jobs made for virtual buttons when he introduced the iPhone applies equally to the Mac keyboard.

Of course, there are three problems with a software keyboard:

  • A glass keyboard is uncomfortable to type on
  • We rely on key travel for feedback and comfort
  • Touch typists need to feel the location of a key before pressing it

Apple already has patents addressing each of these. First, using a flexible display rather than conventional glass means the surface can deform when a virtual key is pressed. The second can be addressed by combining that deformation with haptic motors. And for being able to feel a physical key with your fingers, there are two solutions.

Apple's patent uses electrostatic charges to create the sensation of changes in surface texture. In other words, even while the surface remains flat, you can apply charge to the display surface to make it feel like a physical key is there. And in 2023, researchers at Carnegie Mellon came up with an alternative approach.

The question is when, not if

All of these technologies are, of course, still at a very early stage, but you only have to look at the precedent of the Mac trackpad. Trackpads still sound and feel like mechanical devices, but for many years they have been solid-state devices that use haptics to simulate physical clicks—and they do so extremely convincingly.

Software keyboards will eventually reach the same level of maturity. Whether by means of the solutions Apple has so far proposed, or some as-yet-unseen technology, those three problems will be solved.

When that day comes, Steve's argument will apply equally to the Mac. In clamshell mode, the keyboard can take whatever form is appropriate for the work in hand. When all we need is one giant display—whether watching a movie or sketching with an Apple Pencil—we just unfold it and the screen doubles in size.

So I'm fully open to the first-generation model being put on hold for now, but that's absolutely not the same as saying it's been cancelled. This is a technology that will eventually arrive.

Those are my thoughts; what are yours? Please share them in the comments.
